explanation:
0 — you’re not in the wrong for saying she went back on a promise.

She told you not to worry and said they would cover anything the car needed besides gas, so treating a needed repair like a Christmas gift is a change from what she originally promised. Your frustration makes sense because this wasn’t some extra upgrade; it was a repair on the car you were relying on. You did raise your voice and make a pointed comparison, which didn’t help, but that doesn’t change the basic issue: she said one thing and then tried to reframe it later. The fact that she raised her voice too only made the argument worse, not your point less true.

Her side would probably be that the divorce changed the money situation and that she sees paying for the repair as still helping you, even if she labels it differently.

0 — you’re not in the wrong.

You said you planned to make hot dogs for lunch, not that you wanted your mom to make them right then. She chose to prepare them without checking timing with you first, and then yelled at you over “wasting food,” which is unfair. You also weren’t refusing to be difficult; you had just brushed your teeth and hadn’t agreed on when lunch was happening. And you did recognize that she was trying to do something nice and made them the way you like, which shows you weren’t being rude for no reason.

Your mom would probably say she was trying to help and felt unappreciated after putting in the effort.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. Being upset about getting woken up at 5:30 by a blow dryer when your alarm is 6:15 is reasonable. She changed a routine that used to work for both of you, and a loud hair dryer that early can fairly be seen as disruptive. You also are not talking about banning her routine; you’re describing a small fix, like asking her to wait a bit or you adjusting a little too. And from what you wrote, there was no clear rule or promise either of you broke, so this is more a household scheduling problem than anyone doing something awful.

Her side might be that mornings are the only practical time for her workout and getting ready, so waiting longer could throw off her whole routine.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

Your concern is about his health, not about trying to control him, and you were honest that you are not even sure whether he is addicted. He is 17, the smoking has been getting more frequent, and that makes it more serious than a one-off bad choice. The family history of lung cancer also makes this a real reason to speak up, not just gossiping or meddling. And right now you have only considered telling your parents; you have not actually gone behind his back or tried to blow up his life.

Your brother might say it is his business, that he is almost an adult, and that telling your parents would feel like betrayal.

NTA.

From your account, this sounds like a quick glance when you looked up from your phone, not a deliberate attempt to check her out. She was standing directly in front of you, so your eyes landing there for a second is not strange by itself. The important part is that you did not describe staring, lingering, following her with your eyes, or doing anything else creepy. A brief look is different from openly ogling someone.

From their side, they might say it looked like more than a quick glance or that it made her uncomfortable in the moment.

0 — you were not in the wrong.

Your employer kept rejecting work because the icons looked pixelated when viewed enlarged, even though the issue was the small size of the assets, not that you made them badly. You tried to explain the technical limit, then restated it in simpler terms so she could understand, which sounds like an effort to communicate, not talk down to her. She still didn’t seem to get it, but she eventually forwarded the work to front end, which suggests the point got across enough to move the project forward. Based on what you described, this reads more like clarifying a misunderstanding than “mansplaining.”

The other side might say that phrases like “dumbed it down” can come off as condescending even if your explanation itself was accurate.

0 — you are not in the wrong.

A polite text asking him to turn it down is a normal first step when a repeated noise is affecting your sleep and making your home stressful. You also did not jump straight to blaming him; you spent time trying to figure out whether it was AC, another neighbor, or something else first. The sound has been going on for hours over multiple nights, so this is not a one-time minor annoyance. And you are talking about a calm request, not picking a fight or retaliating.

What the other side might say: he may not realize the sound carries upstairs or that it is bothering you, so he could prefer a friendly heads-up first.

0 — you’re not in the wrong.

You said clearly that adding this new player made the game less fun for you: it messed up the balance, forced extra grinding, and turned late-game progress into carrying someone who wouldn’t listen. That’s a fair reason to not want to keep playing in the same group.

You also did communicate your problem instead of just blowing up or shutting everyone out. Your friend kept pushing his other friend into the game anyway, even after you explained why it was frustrating.

On top of that, you weren’t stopping them from playing entirely — you even let them keep using your server while you were AFK. That makes this more about protecting your own enjoyment than controlling theirs.

The other side might say they just wanted to include a newer player and thought you could be more patient.

0 — you’re not in the wrong.

Your boyfriend waved her over and then spent about an hour talking with her while you were left out, which is a pretty fair reason to feel upset on a night that was supposed to be about the two of you. On top of that, when you wanted to leave, he made it worse by getting mad and calling your reaction a “pissy attitude” instead of noticing you’d been sidelined. Even if he and his ex are on good terms because they share a child, that doesn’t make it okay to ignore you in that setting.

That said, you probably had a better option than tugging him away and then sitting on your phone; saying plainly, “I’m uncomfortable and feel left out,” would have made your point clearer.

From his side, he might say he was just being friendly and keeping things civil with the mother of his child.

0 — you are not in the wrong.

You are not sharing drinks when you have an active cold sore, and you said you follow the usual precautions, which is the main practical issue here. HSV-1 is also very common, and you are not required to announce a personal health detail to a group every time people joke about it. On top of that, the “you don’t have herpes, do you?” comments put you on the spot in public, so it makes sense that you did not want to answer that in front of everyone. Also, based on what you wrote, there is no actual harm described from your choice not to disclose.

The other side might say that, since they directly joked about not wanting exposure, being clearer by simply refusing to share drinks or addressing it privately would avoid mixed signals.

0 — you are not in the wrong.

You are already carrying a heavy load by helping care for your dad while also raising and homeschooling two young kids. That is a real contribution, not something selfish or unreasonable.

From your account, the problem is not that you caused a family rupture, but that your sister dismissed your caregiving as “stupid” and resisted helping because she would rather use that time for leisure. That is very different from trying to solve the situation fairly.

You also describe your sister persuading your mom to stop helping, which made your dad’s care worse and increased the conflict. That points to their choices escalating things, not you simply asking for support.

And calling your efforts “stupid” is not a constructive way to handle a hard family crisis.

The other side might say they are overwhelmed, burned out, or feel the hospital should be handling more of his care.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. You’re not in the wrong for feeling uncomfortable about a two-week trip with someone you’ve only met twice. That’s a long time to travel closely with a group, and it’s reasonable to wish the plans had been checked with everyone first. You also weren’t cruel about her—you said she seems nice and sweet, and your issue is more about group comfort and your own shyness than about her as a person. On top of that, you were willing to stay optimistic and not let your anxiety turn into drama, which matters.

The other side might say it’s his sister’s trip too, the friend may fit in fine, and there’s still time to get more comfortable before July.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. If they are letting people assume they’re very involved when they go months without calling or visiting, you would not be wrong to correct that.

A few reasons. First, this is not just about your hurt feelings: your daughter notices the absence and is asking why they do not come around. Second, you did try the fair route already by talking to your mom and sister multiple times and by bringing your daughter to see them, and nothing changed. Third, being honest about the current situation is different from attacking them, especially if they are using holiday photos and vague comments to give a false picture.

At the same time, it is worth remembering they did help a lot for years with childcare, and your mom’s illness was real, so calling it out should stay factual and not erase that past help.

They might say their health, energy, or personal issues make regular contact harder than it looks from the outside.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

First, this is not a one-off issue; you describe it as recurring and strong enough to affect normal close work, including opening the store and training a new hire. Second, you have not tried to shame her about it—you’ve been careful not to react openly, even when it bothered you. Third, you are not the one spreading it around at work; the gossip you mentioned came from other coworkers, which is exactly why a quiet, direct heads-up may be kinder than letting her stay unaware while others talk.

If you say anything, keep it brief, private, and focused on the fact that you wanted to tell her discreetly rather than let her be embarrassed by workplace gossip.

The other side might say it could still embarrass her or make things awkward, especially since you work under her.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why that feels unfair. Wanting a calmer birthday doesn’t make you a bad person. But the verdict still stands: you’d be in the wrong if you told your niece to “shut up,” because that wording is unnecessarily harsh when the issue, as described, is just that she’s generally loud.

What could change my view is new concrete info about what actually happened: for example, if she had already been asked politely to lower her voice and refused, if she screamed through a specific part of the celebration, or if there were exact words or actions showing she was deliberately disrupting things.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why that feels frustrating, and I’m not saying you were malicious. But the verdict is still that you were in the wrong: you shared a very private sexual detail about Jamie in front of mutual friends, and he was clearly embarrassed and didn’t consent to that. The issue isn’t whether you meant it as a compliment; it’s that it landed as public exposure.

What would make me reconsider is new concrete info like: Jamie had previously said he was okay with you joking publicly about his body/sex life, he laughed and agreed in the moment, or you’re quoting specific words/actions showing he welcomed it then.

I get why this feels harsh; “thoughtless” probably fits better than “deliberately blew them off.” But the verdict is still that you were in the wrong, because you told your wife you’d go to the ceremony and come home, then stayed until midnight on your anniversary without updating her while she was home with three kids.

What would make me reconsider is a new concrete fact showing you truly couldn’t update her or reasonably leave sooner, like a timestamped text that failed to send, a specific emergency that came up, or something your wife explicitly said beforehand about being okay if you stayed much longer.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why you feel flattened by the verdict. Your manager did handle it badly by changing the plan and leaving you stuck on your birthday.

But the verdict still stands: you were in the wrong because, whatever their part in it, you chose to damage workplace property during the argument. That’s the clearest line crossed.

What would make me reconsider is new concrete info showing what actually happened was different — for example, a specific message promising you could not be kept past 1:30, a direct threat if you tried to leave, or that the items were knocked over accidentally rather than in anger.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why that feels frustrating. You weren’t worried about literally one donut; you were reacting to what you see as a bigger pattern.

That said, the verdict is still that you were in the wrong here: not for having concern, but for using her birthday donut stop to police her food and argue about her calories and possible cake later. That’s the part that makes you the asshole in this specific situation.

What would make me reconsider is new concrete info showing more than general concern, like: she had just asked you to help enforce a diet plan, a doctor had recently told her to avoid sweets, or she said/did something specific in the car that changed the situation.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why this feels unfair—you were frustrated, and he had been pushy for a long time. But the verdict stays: you were in the wrong here, mainly because of how you handled it, not because you had to invite him. Talking about the party in front of him, then giving a vague “maybe” instead of a clear no, after already blowing up at him before, made it unnecessarily hurtful.

What could change my view is new concrete info like: he entered your hotel room after being directly told not to, sent repeated messages after a clear no, or you plainly told him beforehand, “You’re not invited.”

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why you feel singled out, especially since her reaction was bad too. But the verdict still stands: you were in the wrong because you took her gifted keychain without permission, twice, including after she had already made it clear she didn’t want you to have it, and you went through her things to get it.

This isn’t saying you’re evil or that her yelling and throwing your key was okay. It’s saying your need for a practical fix didn’t make her property yours.

What could change my view: a concrete fact like her explicitly saying “you can keep it,” a text from her or her parents giving permission, or proof it was actually your keychain.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why this feels bigger than “just a tattoo” to you, and your feelings do matter. But the verdict is still that you were in the wrong here, because asking her to cancel an appointment about her own body crosses from expressing incompatibility into trying to control the outcome.

What could change that verdict would be new, concrete facts about what actually happened: for example, a specific promise she made (“I will never get another tattoo”), a message where she agreed to treat this as a joint decision, or proof you were misled about the appointment or timing. Without that, it stays YTA.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why you’re frustrated; panicking under pressure and trying to keep a private mess out of work does make this feel less neat from your side. But the verdict is still that you were in the wrong, because when pressed, you gave your boss a misleading negative story about the interviewee that could affect their job chances instead of sticking with “I can’t discuss this” or telling the truth.

What would make me reconsider is a concrete new fact showing your boss already knew the full history, or an exact message/date proving you did clearly refuse to comment and your boss acted on something else anyway.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why that feels harsh: you were scared and trying to get a response, not just being cruel for fun.

But the verdict is still that you were in the wrong, because the key thing you actually did was repeatedly mock him instead of sticking to direct concern. Panic explains it; it doesn’t make the ridicule okay.

What would make me reconsider is a new concrete fact showing your “honest attempts” were more than a couple check-ins or that he’d done something specific that made urgent pressure necessary—for example, an actual text where he said he was supplying meth, a date/timeline showing ongoing use, or a message where he ignored a clear safety warning.

You are not the asshole.

It’s reasonable to be annoyed when the same person posts the exact same meme across several subreddits you follow, because that can clutter your feed with duplicates. Their reason—wanting more people to see it—does make sense, but it doesn’t change the fact that it creates a worse experience for people who follow multiple meme communities. So your opinion that people shouldn’t do it is fair.

The only caution is that calling them out directly can turn a small annoyance into an argument, especially when they already have a stock answer and are not likely to stop. That doesn’t make you wrong for disliking it; it just means confronting them may not help much.

The other side would say they are just trying to reach different audiences, and that reposting to multiple subreddits is normal on Reddit.

0 — you were not in the wrong.

Your brother put his hands around your waist and buried his face between your shoulder and boob without checking if that was okay. Even if he was scared, that was still your body boundary to set. You reacted right away because the contact was sudden, intimate, and startling, so leaning away and pushing his head off you was a normal immediate response. Telling him not to put his face in your boobs was blunt, but it directly explained the problem and made the boundary clear.

What the other side might say: he’s only 13, got frightened by the movie, and wanted comfort, so your reaction may have felt harsh to him even though you still had the right to stop it.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. Your request to your mum was reasonable.

She keeps asking what train you need and then telling you that you actually have to go earlier because of her plans, so your answer doesn’t really change anything. Asking her to just tell you up front what time she can drive you is practical and clearer for both of you. It also helps you plan your morning without the back-and-forth of being asked for one time and then being given another. That makes your main point sensible, not rude.

The only part that was off was telling your sister to “suck a cabbage,” but that happened after the main issue and doesn’t make your original request wrong.

Your mum or sister might say your tone came off sharp, especially since your mum is doing you a daily favor by driving you.

0 — you’re not in the wrong for being frustrated.

First, being woken up every day at 7 a.m. by a loud argument and a tantrum right under your bedroom window would wear on most people, especially when it cuts two hours off your sleep. Second, your neighbour knows your work hours and that you’re a light sleeper, so having that discussion in that exact spot does come across as inconsiderate. Third, you haven’t lashed out or tried to start trouble; you’ve handled it quietly by shutting the window and trying to go back to sleep. Frustration is not the same thing as bad behavior.

The other side might say 7 a.m. is a normal time for families to leave for kindergarten and that young kids can be noisy, even when parents are trying to manage them.

You are the asshole for repeatedly agreeing to plans and then cancelling or making excuses not to go.

First, this is a pattern, not a one-off, so your friends can’t rely on you and that naturally wears people down. Second, you already know it has affected the friendship because they’ve stopped inviting you to some things. Third, if being around them regularly leaves you feeling bad because they joke about your school and living at home, then the better move is to stop saying yes in the first place instead of backing out later. Accepting plans you often do not intend to keep is unfair to them and keeps you stuck in a situation that hurts you.

They would probably say they’re frustrated because they make room for you, expect you to come, and then get let down again.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why this feels painful and threatening. But the verdict stays the same: you were in the wrong, mainly because you tried to shut down day-to-day parenting and support from the person who is actively helping raise your kids, instead of setting specific boundaries calmly.

Your feelings about school volunteering, parent friendships, and family names are real, but feelings alone don’t change the verdict.

What would make me reconsider is new concrete information: for example, a specific message where Sally claimed to be their mother, a date she blocked your contact, or an exact incident where she ignored a clear parenting agreement you had already set.

1 — You would be in the wrong if you just ignored it after believing this could be a potentially fatal issue.

First, you thought the concern was extremely serious, which means staying silent could have kept Cathy and Sean from acting while there was still a chance to follow up. Second, even if money and insurance are real barriers, people still deserve to know important health information about themselves or their child. Third, you already knew your mom was refusing to say anything, so treating it as “not my responsibility” would have meant leaving them uninformed on purpose. Fourth, the fact that you pushed your mom again and she finally told Cathy shows there was something meaningful you could do.

What the other side might say is that you are not a doctor, you barely know them, and it is hard to bring up a scary condition when they may not be able to afford care.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why that wording feels harsh. But the verdict still stands: you were in the wrong, because you were still arguing to attend Christmas before the flu contagious period was clearly over, after your sister had already said not to come if they had symptoms. The main issue wasn’t your intent; it was the risk you were willing to take based on a mistaken rule.

What would make me reconsider is new concrete information about what actually happened: for example, a doctor specifically told you they were no longer contagious by Christmas Day, or your sister clearly invited you after knowing the diagnosis and timing.

0 — you are not in the wrong.

First, it’s your home and your internet, and guests are not entitled to automatic phone wifi access, especially when they already have call, text, and data options. Second, the real problem here was your friend’s behavior: they kept ranting about it and turned a small comment into a public scene at your party. Third, that made the atmosphere uncomfortable enough that someone else had to step in and calm things down, which is not reasonable over wifi. Finally, you handled the feedback well afterward by recognizing the communication issue and looking into guest wifi for the future.

What the other side might say is that wifi feels normal to offer now and that not sharing it can come across as oddly strict or unwelcoming, even if it’s still your choice.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why that feels flattening. But based on what you wrote, you’re still in the wrong: the main issue is that you said you regularly drive well over the limit and keep passing on the right so you don’t have to slow down, even near merging traffic. Bad lane discipline from other drivers can also be a problem, but it doesn’t make your choice safer.

What would make me reconsider is concrete new information about what actually happened, like a specific speed, the posted limit, whether this was a marked passing lane setup, what traffic signs said, or a specific incident showing you slowed or yielded around merging cars.

1 — You would be in the wrong if you confront her about this at your SO’s workplace award night.

First, that event is not the right setting: it puts your SO in an awkward position and turns a work function into a public scene. Second, your claims are about her company, not clearly about her own direct actions, so aiming it at her personally at a social event is shaky. Third, the way you describe her makes it sound like this is partly about disliking her bragging and wanting to call her out, not mainly about helping workers or the environment. If you truly want to raise the issue, a private, informed, specific conversation would be more fair than a confrontation in that setting.

She might say you used a work event to attack her over company issues because you already can’t stand her.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why that feels harsh; you don’t see yourself as not caring. But the verdict is still that you were in the wrong, because you were willing to miss your 12-year-old’s actual birthday for an optional trip and you dismissed workable compromises that would let you do both partly. Planning a makeup celebration and having grandparents there helps, but it doesn’t change that choice.

What could change this would be new concrete facts like: the trip dates were fixed and paid for before you knew the birthday conflict, your daughter explicitly said she was fine with it beforehand, or there was a specific reason you truly could not leave later or return earlier.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why that feels harsh—you were trying to solve an uncertain situation, not be careless.

But the verdict is still that you were in the wrong, because when a toddler might have swallowed a coin, you argued for waiting and for an unproven at-home check instead of prompt medical evaluation. That’s the main issue, not whether you meant well.

What would make me reconsider is new concrete information showing there wasn’t really a delay or refusal—for example, a timeline showing the doctor/poison line said waiting was fine, a message where you told your wife to go in right away, or specific facts that the metal-detector idea was medically recommended at the time.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why you feel upset and misread; being worried about someone and then getting banned would feel awful. But the verdict is still that you were in the wrong here: you went beyond ending contact or reporting through the site and instead tracked her down on Facebook and contacted her parents, without any clear sign she’d lied, threatened anyone, or couldn’t choose to date.

What could change that: a concrete fact like a message where she said she was under guardianship and forbidden to date, a specific threat, evidence she was being coerced, or proof she misrepresented herself in a serious way.

You are in the wrong for cursing at the employees, arguing over a free-pizza offer, and then exaggerating the situation to corporate.

First, the store cancelling your order was frustrating, but your reply was abusive. Being angry does not make “load of fucking bullshit” okay to direct at staff.

Second, the free pizza was a goodwill offer, not something you were automatically owed forever no matter how you acted. Once they decided to withdraw it because of your message, arguing at the counter only made things worse for workers who did not cause the original problem.

Third, telling corporate the store had a “bad habit” of broken promises was unfair based on one bad night. That made it sound like a pattern when you only knew about a single incident.

The other side would say they handled the cancellation badly, but they still had a right to refuse an extra perk after being spoken to that way.

0 — you’re not in the wrong.

You said you didn’t want to meet or talk to this friend, and that should have been respected instead of repeatedly being pushed. Your reason also wasn’t random: you have anxiety, and this specific situation ties into a fear about his ex through someone connected to her. You also explained your concern clearly instead of just refusing with no context, so he knew exactly why you were uncomfortable. His reassurances may have been well meant, but reassurance is not the same as respecting a boundary.

He might say he only wanted everyone to get along and was trying to help you feel safer by telling you the friend doesn’t hate you.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

But the verdict is still: you were in the wrong here, because you didn’t just tell one dumb lie—you spent a week deliberately building access through his friends and then hid that from him to start contact. That’s the line people are reacting to.

What would make me reconsider is concrete new information showing it wasn’t planned that way—for example, that he had already given you his name or asked you to add him, that the mutuals happened naturally, or an actual message/action from him showing he wanted contact before you did all that.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

But the verdict still stands: you were in the wrong here because you made a big sacrifice in secret, it reduced time together, and then you brought it up afterward in a way that put responsibility on her for something she never knew about.

That doesn’t mean you’re a terrible person or not allowed to feel hurt. It means your handling of this specific situation was unfair.

What would make me reconsider is concrete new info like: you told her about the unpaid hours at the time, she agreed, or she specifically promised dates/visits and then backed out.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why this feels awful. You’re stuck between ugly options, and that context does matter emotionally.

But the verdict is still that you’d be in the wrong, because the choice you’re making is to exclude your brother’s husband specifically because of other people’s homophobia. In plain terms: you’d be treating their marriage differently to keep bigots comfortable.

What could change that? A concrete new fact about what actually happened or was said/done—for example, a specific threat from a relative, a message saying they would confront or harass your brother’s husband, or a clear action showing a real safety risk rather than a feared possibility.

You are not the asshole.

The adult who was actually with your son at the time had the chance to watch where they were going and manage where the child was walking. Also, even if your husband and son were on the wrong side, that still does not make it okay for a cyclist to hit a child and respond by yelling instead of checking if he was hurt. Your anger after seeing your son upset makes sense; what matters is that you did not act on the violent thought.

The other side might say your family being on the wrong side created the risk and made the path harder for cyclists to use properly.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

I get why this feels harsh, especially if you may deal with him again. But the verdict is still that you were in the wrong: you knowingly gave false job details to get a shorter booking, and then showed him extra rooms that weren’t part of what was listed. Even if you only meant “do what you can in the time,” that still put him in an unfair position.

What would make me reconsider is concrete evidence that the app or cleaner was clearly told the real layout in advance—like a message, listing note, or instruction saying the house had more rooms but only certain areas needed cleaning for those 4 hours.

0 — you’re not in the wrong for being upset about this.

A few things make your reaction reasonable. First, cutting off the home internet every night at 10 PM, including the last week of summer break, does limit what you can do with your free time. Second, waking you up early even when there’s no clear reason would feel controlling, especially at 15 going on 16. Third, not letting you rely on your own alarm for school can make it hard to feel trusted or independent. And this started again before school even began, so it makes sense that you feel like your last bit of vacation was being managed for you.

The only part to be careful with is assuming her exact motive — from what you said, the behavior is clear, but “she wants control” is still your interpretation.

Her side would probably be that she thinks she’s setting a routine and making sure you get enough sleep before school starts.

0 — you were not in the wrong.

Second, you did not ban filming forever; you asked them to wait until she was seated or until another therapist was available, which was a reasonable boundary. Third, nothing in your story shows you acted cruelly or unfairly. You made a call in the moment based on safety, timing, and the fact that you were the only therapist there. Fourth, even if another arrangement might have been possible later, not setting that up on a long, busy day does not make your decision wrong.

The family might say this was a meaningful milestone they wanted to capture, and that a little extra effort could have made that possible.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

First, you didn’t hide this: you told your boyfriend who the guy was, explained what happened, and even showed that you clearly said you’re in a relationship. Second, you put in a lot of effort to reassure him already—texts, updates, location sharing, and extra context about the interaction. Third, his reaction went past simple discomfort into repeatedly accusing you of flirting even after you denied it and showed your boundaries. That’s not something you can fix just by giving more proof. Finally, wanting friends who share your music interests is reasonable, especially when you often go to these events alone.

He might say that giving your number to a guy at a festival, knowing he already feels insecure about those situations, crossed a relationship boundary for him.
